headline: Two algorithm-policy profiles, and a two-digit year read against the clock rather than a constant.
summary: `pki.lint` gains the two profiles an operator needs to ask whether a certificate will still be acceptable after a transition date: `nist-pqc-transition` for NIST IR 8547's 2030 and 2035 transitions, and `cnsa-2.0` for the CNSA 2.0 suite profile, which also reaches `pki.lint.crl` and `pki.lint.ocsp` because the document states its signature rule once for all three. Neither is detected: which algorithm policy a certificate is held to is the caller's assertion, so both are inert until named. Alongside them, an HTTP `Retry-After` carrying the obsolete two-digit-year date format is read against the time the value arrives, which is what RFC 7231 requires and what a fixed cutoff stops being after the year it was chosen in.

Added: `pki.lint.certificate(der, { profile: "nist-pqc-transition" })` reports NIST IR 8547's two transitions. A classical subject public key or signature algorithm in a certificate issued from 2036 is an error, which Table 2 and Table 4 make disallowed at every parameter set they list. A classical subject key at or below the 112-bit security strength issued from 2031 is a warning, which is the strength those tables deprecate and which SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 Table 2 maps onto an RSA modulus of 2048 bits, a curve whose field is 224 to 255 bits, and a finite-field group stated as a pair, L of 2048 with N of 224. Either finite-field parameter caps the strength, so a group with a 3072-bit prime and a 224-bit subgroup order is reported, and a group whose encoding states no subgroup order is read on its prime. "After 2030" and "after 2035" name whole years, so each transition begins on 1 January of the year that follows and is compared against the certificate's own notBefore. IR 8547 is an initial public draft, so these are a draft's dates and the citation says so.

Ed25519 is deliberately outside the 2031 row. Its field is 255 bits, which SP 800-57's ECC column places at the 112-bit strength, so reading the two documents together would deprecate it after 2030; IR 8547's own EdDSA row carries a 128-bit entry alone, with no 112-bit entry and no 2030 date, and the profile follows the document it cites. A composite signature or subject key is passed over in both rows, because the tables list pure families and the same guidance endorses dual-algorithm operation through the transition.

`pki.lint.certificate(der, { profile: "cnsa-2.0" })` reports the CNSA 2.0 certificate profile of `draft-jenkins-cnsa2-pkix-profile-05`, which states what a certificate must carry where the NSA algorithm notice lists algorithms. Fifteen rows: the subject public key must be ML-DSA-87 or ML-KEM-1024 and the signature must be id-ml-dsa-87, which also answers the clause forbidding HashML-DSA, since a HashML-DSA identifier is not that one; a keyUsage extension must be critical in all three scopes; a self-signed CA must carry a subjectKeyIdentifier, a keyUsage and a basicConstraints, a non-self-signed CA an authorityKeyIdentifier, a keyUsage and a basicConstraints, where a certificate whose keyUsage asserts keyCertSign is read as a CA whether or not it carries basicConstraints, since RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.3 requires the cA boolean of any certificate asserting that bit and a certificate omitting the extension is the one this requirement is about; a CA reissued in its own name under a new key is read as the second of the two CA kinds, since its authorityKeyIdentifier names a key other than its own subjectKeyIdentifier and the section governing it permits the pathLenConstraint the self-signed section forbids; and an end entity an authorityKeyIdentifier and a keyUsage, with a missing subjectKeyIdentifier on an end entity reported as a warning where that clause says SHOULD; a CA's basicConstraints must be critical and a self-signed CA's must carry no pathLenConstraint, which the non-self-signed section calls optional; a CA's keyUsage must set keyCertSign and cRLSign, may set digitalSignature and nonRepudiation, and must set nothing else; an end entity's extKeyUsage must be present and must not name anyExtendedKeyUsage; and a certificatePolicies extension must be non-critical and should carry no policy qualifiers. Each departure from a closed key-usage set is its own finding, so a certificate setting two forbidden bits reports both.

The end entity key-usage set follows the kind the subject public key declares, which is what makes that clause readable from the bytes: an ML-DSA-87 certificate must set digitalSignature and may set nonRepudiation, an ML-KEM-1024 certificate must set keyEncipherment alone, and a key outside the suite has no set to be held to and is reported as the key instead.

`pki.lint.crl` and `pki.lint.ocsp` take the same `cnsa-2.0` name for the one rule the document states about them: the signature on a CRL and on an OCSP response follows the same rule as a certificate's. One rule, written once, in each of its three homes.

Every clause of that profile which this toolkit's parsers settle before a row could read it has a conformance vector asserting the parser's verdict instead: a version other than 3 arrives as `x509/bad-version`, a present parameters field on either suite algorithm as `x509/bad-algorithm-parameters`, and an inner TBSCertificate or TBSCertList signature identifier that differs from the outer signatureAlgorithm as `x509/bad-signature-algorithm` or `crl/bad-signature-algorithm`, so the row reading one of those two fields answers for both. Three further clauses are recorded without a row, because the bytes do not settle them: which extended key purposes are consistent with which key-usage bits is enumerated nowhere in the document, a certificatePolicies extension that is present asserts a policy, and the responder authorization an OCSP response also owes is a trust decision over a chain that `pki.ocsp.verify` makes.
Fixed: `pki.lint.certificate`, `pki.lint.crl`, `pki.lint.ocsp`, `pki.lint.csr`, `pki.lint.cms`, `pki.lint.tsp` and `pki.lint.attrcert` all answer the same way about where a profile name lives. A verb handed a profile it does not run refuses it with `lint/unknown-profile` naming every verb that does run it, read from the registry rather than from a list written into each verb. Before, each verb carried its own chain of checks in its own order, so a name carried by more than one artifact drew a different answer depending on which verb was asked, and each chain omitted the artifacts nobody had added a branch for: a CMS profile name reached `pki.lint.crl` as simply unknown. `pki.lint.rules(profile, artifact)` gives that same sentence, so asking where a profile lives and asking a verb to run it are one answer.

An HTTP `Retry-After` header carrying an rfc850-date, the obsolete format with a two-digit year, is read against the time the value arrives. RFC 7231 section 7.1.1.1 requires a recipient to read a year more than 50 years in the future as the most recent past year with the same two digits, which depends on when the value is received. A caller that supplied a reference time already got that; one that did not fell back to a fixed cutoff at 70, which is the same rule evaluated once for a reference year around 2020 and which misreads a band of years that widens by one every year. At a 2026 receipt the years 70 through 76 were read a century early. `pki.est`'s retry handling is the reachable caller, since its own `now` option is optional. The four-digit formats are unaffected.

`pki.rfc3339`'s description of why it validates the calendar names the case that needs it. `2026-02-30T00:00:00Z` is the one the runtime accepts and reads as 2 March, two days from the date the value names; month 13, hour 25 and a `+25:00` offset are refused by the runtime as well, so the check agrees with it there. A `:60` leap second, which the description gave as its example, is one of those, and refusing it is a decision rather than a malformation: RFC 3339 section 5.7 permits the value and JavaScript cannot represent it. Each of those statements now has a vector asserting it against the runtime, so the reason the check exists cannot quietly stop being true. No behavior changed.
Changed: `pki.lint.profiles()` lists `nist-pqc-transition` and `cnsa-2.0` beside the others. `cnsa-2.0` appears once although three verbs run it, because that call enumerates profile names rather than the places they are registered.
